newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY JEWS CLAIM VICTIMS' ASSETS IN SWISS BANKS.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY JEWS CLAIM VICTIMS' ASSETS IN SWISS BANKS.

text.p: Hungary's Jewish communities on Friday announced their claim for assets held by Hungarian Jews, who were killed by the Nazis, on bank accounts in Switzerland.

The Hungarian Television said the Budapest office of the World Jewish Congress (WJC) asked Hungarian Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs in a letter on Friday to inform WJC about the content of agreements, which affected Jewish Holocaust victims' property, with Switzerland.

Lajos Bakos, director of WJC's Budapest office told the television that the Hungarian Jewish communities had a claim for holocaust victims' assets, which the current investigation on the agreements would unveil.
"The assets, which the investigation will uncover, could be added to the property of the foundation to be set up by Hungary for the compensation of Jews," he said.
Hungary said earlier this month that it concluded 20 property rights agreements in the late 1940s and early 1950s with 17 Western countries.

The accords dealt with the payment of war reparations by Hungary, a World War Two ally of Nazi Germany, as well as compensation for Western-owned property nationalised by the Communist government which took power in 1949.
Hungary has also acknowledged recently that it signed a similar agreement with Switzerland in 1973, involving 325,000 Swiss francs ($259,200) on bank deposits of Jews who perished in World War Two.
The Hungarian government is searching for the agreements and the related letters and other documents, which explain the agreements, and have promised to publish them soon.
Bakos did not say how much lost Jewish property WJC hoped for the investigation to find.
He said Hungarian Jewish communities planned to spend the money to be generated from the returning assets for education and charity.
Some 600,000 of Hungary's 800,000 Jews perished in Nazi labour or concentration camps. There are an estimated 100,000 Jews in Hungary today, including 20,000 Holocaust survivors.

Swiss banks, accused by Jewish groups of sitting on the wealth of Holocaust victims, on Friday called a news conference for November 12 to discuss the status of the search on behalf of some 1,000 claimants seeking assets their relatives may have put in secretive Swiss banks.
